# Display Device with Integrated Touch Sensing

## Dual-Purpose Counter Electrodes

The display device employs an innovative architecture in which counter electrodes serve two distinct functions. During display operations, these electrodes act as common electrodes, providing the reference voltage necessary for controlling the liquid crystal or display medium. During touch sensing operations, the same electrodes function as scan electrodes, detecting user input by measuring changes in capacitance. This dual-purpose design eliminates the need for a separate touch sensing layer, thereby reducing the overall thickness and complexity of the device.

## Time-Division Frame Structure

To accommodate both display and touch sensing functions using shared electrodes, each frame period is divided into distinct time segments. Each frame contains a write period, during which the screen is continuously scanned to update the displayed image, followed by a touch sensing period. The touch sensing periods are positioned between consecutive write periods, allowing the device to alternate between refreshing the display content and detecting touch input. This time-division approach ensures that both operations can be performed without interference, using the same physical electrodes at different moments within each frame.

## Dual Scan Circuit Configuration

The device incorporates two separate scan circuits to manage its various operations. The first scan circuit is responsible for scanning the gate lines, sequentially activating rows of pixels to enable data writing during the display process. The second scan circuit is dedicated to scanning the counter electrodes, coordinating their operation for both display and touch sensing functions. This separation of scanning responsibilities allows for precise and independent control of each electrode set.

## Structure of the Second Scan Circuit

The second scan circuit is composed of two principal components: a shift register unit and a switch unit. The shift register unit generates the timing signals required to sequentially address the counter electrodes. The switch unit, which selectively routes the appropriate drive signals to the counter electrodes, includes two key transistors. A seventh thin-film transistor is configured to output a DC drive signal, which is used to supply a stable common voltage during display operations. An eighth thin-film transistor is configured to output an AC drive signal, which is used to excite the counter electrodes during touch sensing operations. By switching between these two transistors, the circuit can supply the correct type of signal appropriate to each phase of the frame.

## Voltage Stabilization During the Write Period

To ensure reliable operation during the display phase, a second control signal is applied during the write period. This control signal fixes the voltage at a third retention node, which is connected to the gate electrode of the seventh thin-film transistor. By maintaining a stable voltage at this node, the device ensures that the seventh thin-film transistor remains in its intended state, allowing the DC drive signal to be consistently output to the counter electrodes throughout the write period. This voltage stabilization prevents unwanted fluctuations that could otherwise degrade display quality or cause erratic behavior in the switching operation.

# Integrated Touch-Display Device with Dual-Function Counter Electrodes

## Overview

The present disclosure describes a display device that achieves an efficient integration of display and touch-sensing functionality through a novel electrode architecture. Rather than employing separate electrode layers for display operation and touch detection, this device utilizes counter electrodes that serve a dual purpose: functioning as common electrodes during the display phase and as scan electrodes during the touch-sensing phase. This integrated approach reduces the overall complexity, thickness, and manufacturing cost of the display panel while maintaining reliable performance in both operational modes.

## Electrode and Scanning Architecture

The device incorporates two distinct scanning circuits to manage its dual functionality. The first scan circuit is dedicated to driving the gate lines of the display, controlling the row-by-row addressing of pixels during image rendering. The second scan circuit is responsible for scanning the counter electrodes, coordinating their behavior across the different operational periods within each frame.

The second scan circuit is composed of two principal components:

- **A shift register unit**, which sequentially generates the timing signals required to scan the counter electrodes in an ordered progression.
- **A switch unit**, which includes dedicated thin-film transistors (TFTs) configured to selectively apply either DC drive signals or AC drive signals to the counter electrodes, depending on the current operational mode.

This arrangement allows the counter electrodes to receive the appropriate signal type at the appropriate time—a stable DC reference voltage when acting as common electrodes for display, and an alternating drive signal when acting as scan electrodes for touch sensing.

## Frame-Based Operation

Each frame of operation is divided into two temporal segments: a **write period** and a **touch-sensing period**. During the write period, the display device performs its image-updating function, with the counter electrodes serving as common electrodes to establish the reference voltage necessary for driving the liquid crystal or pixel elements. During the subsequent touch-sensing period, the same counter electrodes are repurposed as scan electrodes, enabling the detection of touch inputs across the panel surface.

By time-multiplexing these two functions within a single frame, the device ensures that display refresh and touch detection can coexist without requiring separate physical structures for each.

## Reliable Mode Switching via Node Voltage Control

A key aspect of the design lies in its ability to reliably transition between display and touch-sensing functions. To achieve this, a **second control signal** is applied to fix the voltage of a **third retention node** during the write period. By stabilizing the potential at this node, the circuit prevents unintended state changes or signal interference that could otherwise arise from the transition between the two operational modes.

This voltage-fixing mechanism ensures that the switch unit's thin-film transistors respond correctly and predictably, allowing for clean and dependable switching between the DC drive signals used for display and the AC drive signals used for touch sensing.

## Advantages

Through this integrated architecture, the display device offers several benefits:

1. **Structural efficiency** — By using the counter electrodes for both display and touch functions, the design eliminates the need for a separate touch-sensing electrode layer.
2. **Reliable operation** — The controlled fixing of the retention node voltage guarantees stable transitions between operational modes.
3. **Coordinated timing** — The combination of the first and second scan circuits enables precise management of gate line driving and counter electrode scanning within each frame.

In summary, the described device provides an efficient and reliable integrated touch-display architecture that combines display and touch-sensing capabilities into a unified electrode structure, leveraging carefully coordinated scanning circuitry and node voltage control to deliver dependable dual-mode performance.

# Patent Abstract

## Display Device with Integrated Touch Sensing and Common Electrodes

**Abstract**

A display device is disclosed that integrates touch sensing functionality with common electrodes to reduce panel thickness and manufacturing complexity. The display device comprises a plurality of common electrodes arranged in a display region, wherein each common electrode is configured to operate in a time-division multiplexed manner, functioning as a display electrode during a display period and as a touch sensing electrode during a touch sensing period.

The device further includes a scan circuit configured to sequentially supply scan signals to the common electrodes during the touch sensing period. In one configuration, the scan circuit comprises a plurality of shift register stages coupled to respective common electrodes, each stage generating a corresponding drive signal for touch detection.

A thin-film transistor (TFT) switch configuration is provided, wherein a plurality of TFT switches selectively couple each common electrode to either a common voltage line or a touch sensing signal line based on a control signal. During the display period, the TFT switches connect the common electrodes to the common voltage line to establish a reference potential for display operation. During the touch sensing period, the TFT switches connect the common electrodes to the touch sensing signal line, enabling the common electrodes to transmit and receive touch drive signals.

The control signal is supplied by a timing controller that coordinates switching between the display period and the touch sensing period. By reusing the common electrodes for both display and touch sensing functions and controlling signal routing through the TFT switches, the display device achieves an integrated in-cell touch structure with reduced component count, improved touch sensitivity, and a thinner form factor.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the technical operation of an in-cell touch display where counter electrodes serve dual purposes for display and touch sensing.
counterfactuals.output:
# In-Cell Touch Display: Technical Operation

## Core Concept

In-cell touch technology integrates the touch sensing function directly into the LCD/display stack, rather than using a separate touch layer on top. The key innovation is the **dual-purpose use of the common electrode (VCOM)**, which traditionally serves only display functions but is repurposed for touch sensing.

## Dual Role of Counter Electrodes

The **common electrode (VCOM)** performs two functions:

1. **Display function** — provides a common reference voltage across the pixel array to control liquid crystal orientation (working with the pixel electrodes to modulate light)

2. **Touch sensing function** — acts as capacitive sensing electrodes to detect finger position

## Time-Division Multiplexing

Because the same electrodes cannot perform both tasks simultaneously, operation is **time-multiplexed** within each display frame:

| Phase | Function | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| **Display period** | VCOM as common electrode | Standard image rendering; VCOM held at reference voltage |
| **Touch period** | VCOM as touch sensor | Electrode segments driven/sensed for touch detection |

The frame is divided so display refresh and touch scanning alternate rapidly enough to be imperceptible to the user.

## Electrode Segmentation

- The single continuous VCOM layer is **divided into a grid of segmented blocks/patches**
- During touch mode, these segments function as **self-capacitance or mutual-capacitance electrodes**
- Each segment connects to touch sensing circuitry via routing lines

## Capacitive Sensing Mechanism

- **Self-capacitance:** Each electrode segment measures capacitance-to-ground; a finger increases capacitance, revealing X-Y coordinates
- **Mutual-capacitance:** Segmented VCOM acts as drive/sense electrodes; a finger disturbs the coupling capacitance between intersections

## Key Technical Advantages

- **Reduced thickness** — eliminates a separate touch sensor layer
- **Better optical clarity** — fewer stacked layers reduce reflection/light loss
- **Lower cost** at scale (fewer components/lamination steps)

## Design Challenges

- **Display-touch interference** — display signals can couple noise into touch sensing; time-multiplexing and shielding mitigate this
- **Synchronization complexity** — requires tight coordination between the display driver and touch controller (often integrated as a **TDDI chip** — Touch and Display Driver Integration)
- **Signal-to-noise management** — proximity to display circuitry demands careful filtering

---

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe how a display device separates write periods and touch sensing periods within one frame, including the role of shift registers and TFT switches.
counterfactuals.output:
# Time-Division Multiplexing in Touch Display Devices

Modern touch displays (particularly in-cell and on-cell designs) often share electrodes and driving periods between display and touch functions. To avoid interference between these operations, the device divides each frame into distinct time segments.

## Frame Division Structure

Within a single frame period, the timing controller partitions the time into two categories of intervals:

**Display (Write) Periods**
- Pixel data is written to the display panel
- Gate lines are scanned sequentially to charge pixels
- Common electrodes function as display reference voltage

**Touch Sensing Periods**
- Display driving is paused
- Shared electrodes are repurposed as touch sensors
- Capacitance changes are measured to detect touch

These periods are typically interleaved (e.g., several display segments alternating with touch segments) so both operations complete within the frame time, keeping refresh rates stable.

## Role of Shift Registers

The **shift register** (part of the gate driver / GIP circuit) generates the sequential scanning signals:

- During **write periods**, the shift register propagates a pulse from stage to stage, sequentially activating gate lines to write image data row by row.
- When a **touch period** begins, the shift register operation is **paused or held**. Its clock signals are stopped, freezing the scanning progress.
- When the display period resumes, the shift register **continues from where it stopped**, ensuring no rows are skipped and image integrity is preserved.

This pause-and-resume capability lets the panel "share" the frame time without losing scan continuity.

## Role of TFT Switches

**Thin-film transistor (TFT) switches** act as gates that route signals to the appropriate function:

- **Pixel TFTs**: Each pixel's TFT is turned ON by the gate line during writing, allowing data voltage to charge the pixel storage capacitor. During touch periods, these TFTs are OFF, isolating and holding the stored pixel charge.

- **Multiplexing/routing TFTs**: Additional switching transistors connect the shared electrodes to either:
  - The **display driver** (supplying common voltage Vcom) during write periods, or
  - The **touch sensing circuit** during touch periods.

A control signal toggles these switches to reconfigure the electrode connections between the two modes.

## Summary of Operation

1. **Write period** → Shift register scans → Gate lines turn ON pixel TFTs → Data written → Electrodes held at Vcom.
2. **Transition** → Shift register held → Routing TFTs switch electrode connections.
3. **Touch period** → Sensing circuit reads electrode capacitance → Pixel TFTs OFF (charge retained).
4. **Resume** → Shift register continues scanning the next rows.

This coordinated timing allows a single panel to perform both display and touch functions without cross-talk, using the shift register for scan continuity and TFT switches for signal routing.

# Second Scan Circuit for Counter Electrode Drive

## Overview

A second scan circuit is used in display technologies (particularly in some LCD and OLED architectures) to selectively drive counter electrodes (common electrodes) using a combination of DC and AC signals routed through thin-film transistors (TFTs).

## Basic Circuit Structure

### Core Components

**1. Thin-Film Transistors (TFTs)**
- Act as switching elements
- Gate terminals connected to scan lines
- Source/drain terminals connect signal lines to counter electrodes
- Typically arranged in a matrix corresponding to display pixels or regions

**2. Signal Supply Lines**
- **DC signal line**: Provides a constant reference voltage
- **AC signal line**: Provides an alternating/oscillating drive signal

**3. Counter Electrodes**
- The target electrodes being driven
- Connected to TFT output terminals

## Signal Routing Configuration

```
Scan Line (Gate) ──┬──────┬──────┬──
                   │      │      │
                 [TFT]  [TFT]  [TFT]
                   │      │      │
   DC/AC ──────────┴──────┴──────┴── Counter Electrodes
   Signal Lines
```

## Operational Structure

### Selective Switching Mechanism

The second scan circuit typically enables:

1. **DC Mode Operation**
   - When TFTs are activated in DC configuration
   - Provides stable reference potential to counter electrodes
   - Used during certain display periods or for specific pixels

2. **AC Mode Operation**
   - TFTs route AC signals to counter electrodes
   - Prevents charge accumulation and image sticking
   - Enables inversion drive schemes

### Multiplexing Approach

The circuit often uses TFTs to **selectively connect** either:
- DC signal source → counter electrode, OR
- AC signal source → counter electrode

based on the scan timing and driving requirements.

## Typical Advantages

| Feature | Benefit |
|---------|---------|
| TFT switching | Precise timing control |
| DC/AC combination | Flexible drive schemes |
| Second scan structure | Independent counter electrode control |

---

# Abstract

A touch-integrated display device is disclosed, comprising a display panel having a plurality of gate lines and a plurality of counter electrodes that function both as common electrodes during a display period and as touch sensing electrodes during a touch sensing period. The device includes a first scan circuit configured to sequentially supply scan signals to the plurality of gate lines and a second scan circuit configured to selectively drive the plurality of counter electrodes for touch sensing.

The first scan circuit and the second scan circuit are controlled by a plurality of control signals, including at least a first clock signal and a start pulse signal for the gate line scanning operation, and a second clock signal and an enable signal for the counter electrode driving operation. Each scan circuit comprises a plurality of cascaded stages, wherein each stage includes a retention node (Q node) configured to maintain a voltage level for controlling an output transistor, and an inverting retention node (QB node) configured to maintain a complementary voltage level for controlling a pull-down operation.

The retention nodes are charged and discharged in response to the control signals, and a stabilization circuit is coupled to each retention node to reduce leakage current and prevent voltage fluctuation during a hold period. In one embodiment, the second scan circuit shares timing synchronization with the first scan circuit such that the counter electrode driving during the touch sensing period is time-division multiplexed with the gate line scanning during the display period, thereby reducing signal interference and improving touch sensing accuracy.

The disclosed configuration enables reduced bezel width, simplified circuit architecture, and enhanced display and touch performance in an integrated touch display panel.
